title: String or Array? Yes!
summary: Introduces the concept that a string is fundamentally an array of characters terminated by a null character.
main_text: String or Array? Yes! Now that we know about arrays, you might realize that a string looks CONSPICUOUSLY like an array of characters! A string constant is an array of chars that ends with a null char. The string "CS 102" is equivalent to a character array with indices [0] through [6] containing: 'C', 'S', ' ', '1', '0', '2', '\0'. The null character '\0' marks the end of the string.
notes_text: This is the key insight that connects prior array knowledge to string representation. The null terminator is critical for C-style strings.

images.description: Diagram showing the string "CS 102" mapped to a character array with index positions [0] through [6], where each cell contains one character: 'C', 'S', ' ', '1', '0', '2', '\0'. A double arrow connects the string literal to the array representation.

title: Initializing Character Arrays
summary: Shows how to initialize character arrays using comma-separated character lists or string literals, and explains that the compiler can infer array size from initialization.
main_text: Initializing Character Arrays. We can store a string in an array of chars. We can either use a comma separate list of chars or just a string in double quotes ("). If an initialization list is provided you need not specify the size in the square brackets (i.e. just use empty []) as the compiler can figure out what size the array must be by counting the initial values. Code examples: int data[5] = {9, 7, 8, 9, 5}; double dec[4] = {0.25, 0.3}; (remaining elements initialized to 0). char str1[3] = {'C', 'S', '\0'}; For char arrays easier to use "". char str2[3] = "CS"; str2 initialization is same as str1. char str3[] = "CS"; allocates array of size 3. char str4[] = "How long is this string?!"; allocates array of size 26. Specifying sizes is not necessary when using initial values list.
notes_text: Note that the dec array shows partial initialization where unspecified elements default to 0. The str1 and str2 examples show two equivalent ways to initialize character arrays.

images.description: Two memory diagrams showing array contents: the data array with values 9,7,8,9,5 at indices [0]-[4], and the dec array with values 0.25, 0.3, 0, 0 at indices [0]-[3]. Also a small diagram showing str1 as an empty array.

title: Character Arrays and Strings (1)
summary: Explains how C/C++ string constants are character arrays ending with a null character, introduces the term C-String, and demonstrates printing and modifying character arrays.
main_text: Character Arrays and Strings (1). In C/C++, string constants (the text in between " ") are just character arrays. Each character consumes 1 element in the array. Ends with the null character (e.g. 0 decimal or '\0' ASCII). This approach of using an array of char's to store a string is referred to as a C-String because there was no string type in C (i.e. before C++). Code example: #include <string>. using namespace std; int main() { char str1[3] = {'C', 'S', '\0'}; char str2[7] = "CS 102"; cout << str1 << endl; // prints "CS". cout << str2 << endl; // prints "CS 102". str2[5] = '3'; cout << str2 << endl; // prints "CS 103". return 0; } Program Output: CS, CS 102, CS 103, hello. Memory diagram shows str2 at addresses 520-526 with indices [0]-[6] containing 'C','S',' ','1','0','2','\0'.
notes_text: The term C-String is important to distinguish from the C++ string type introduced later. Individual characters can be modified using array indexing.

images.description: Memory diagram showing str2 stored in computer memory at addresses 520-526, with indices [0]-[6], containing characters 'C', 'S', ' ', '1', '0', '2', '\0'.

title: Strings Before C++
summary: Contrasts how strings were handled in C (character arrays only) versus C++ which introduced the string type to solve character array issues.
main_text: Strings Before C++. Before there was C++, there was C! In C, the string type did NOT exist! Only character arrays. C++ introduced the string type to solve many of the issues that character arrays have. (Detailed in the next slides). C example: char s1[6]="CS102" with a 'no' symbol next to the word 'string' indicating no string type available. C++ example: char s1[6]="CS102" and also string s = "CS102" showing both options are available.
notes_text: This slide sets up the motivation for why C++ strings were created. The limitations of C-strings will be explored in the following slides.

images.description: Visual comparison showing the C language logo with only char array syntax available (with a prohibition symbol on the word 'string'), and the C++ logo showing both char array and string type syntax available.

title: Where Does It End?
summary: Uses an analogy of fans in a crowd to motivate the concept of string boundaries and the need for a termination marker.
main_text: Where Does It End? In this picture, look at a row of fans. Where does one friend group end and another group of friends start? The slide shows a photograph of USC football fans in a stadium crowd, wearing cardinal and gold colors, with letters spelling 'FIGHT ON USC' painted on their chests. The analogy illustrates the difficulty of determining boundaries without explicit markers, motivating why strings need a null terminator.
notes_text: This is a motivational slide using an analogy. Just as you cannot tell where one group of friends ends in a crowd without a marker, the computer needs the null character to know where a string ends in memory.

images.description: Photograph of USC football fans in a stadium, wearing cardinal and gold, with letters painted on their chests spelling 'FIGHT ON USC'. Used as an analogy for why strings need explicit end markers.

title: Character Arrays and Loops
summary: Demonstrates how to iterate through character arrays using loops, and explains that cout and cin have built-in loops for handling character arrays.
main_text: Character Arrays and Loops. How many things can a computer do at a time? To printout a string/character array, we'd have to print one character at a time! But C/C++ treats character arrays specially. cout has a loop inside its code to print strings/character arrays. How does it know when to stop? The null char! Though not shown, cin also has a loop inside to input a string. We say cout and cin have a special relationship with character arrays. Code example: char str1[7] = "CS 102"; for(int i=0; str1[i] != '\0'; i++) { cout << str1[i]; } cout << endl; // but cout has its own loop so you don't have to write the loop above but just what you see below. cout << str1 << endl; // prints "CS 102". Program Output: CS 102, CS 102. Memory diagram shows str1 at addresses 520-526 with contents 'C','S',' ','1','0','2','\0'.
notes_text: The loop condition str1[i] != '\0' is key to understanding how C-strings are processed. The null terminator serves as the loop's stopping condition.

images.description: Memory diagram showing str1 stored at addresses 520-526, indices [0]-[6], containing 'C','S',' ','1','0','2','\0' in computer memory.

title: cout's Special Relationship with Character Arrays
summary: Explains that cout automatically loops through character arrays to print them, unlike other array types which require manual loops.
main_text: cout's Special Relationship with Character Arrays. To print out all elements of any array type OTHER than a character array (i.e. int, double, bool, etc.) you must write your OWN loop (i.e. because computers can only do 1 thing at a time). But for character arrays, you can just give cout the name of the array and it will use its own INTERNAL loop to print out all characters for you. So, internally it is actually looping over the characters so you don't have to. It just assumes when you give it a character array that you WANT it to print out all the characters in the array. Thus, we say cout treats character arrays specially. Code example: int data[5] = {9, 7, 8, 9, 5}; char str1[] = "Many chars"; for(int i=0; i < 5; i++){ cout << data[i] << " "; } cout << endl; // doesn't work for an int, double or any other type of array. cout << data << endl; // cout treats char. arrays specially. cout << str1 << endl; Program Output: 9 7 8 9 5, 0x7fffce40, Many chars.
notes_text: Note that printing an int array name directly outputs its memory address (0x7fffce40), not its contents. This contrasts with character arrays where the name prints the string contents.

images.description: Two memory diagrams: one showing data array with values 9,7,9,9,5 at indices [0]-[4], and one showing str1 array with 'M','a',...,'s','\0' at indices [0]-[10].

title: cin's Special Relationship with Character Arrays
summary: Explains that cin automatically reads an entire string into a character array, stopping at the next space, unlike other array types which require element-by-element input.
main_text: cin's Special Relationship with Character Arrays. To get input for all elements of an array type OTHER than character arrays (i.e. int, double, etc.) you must write your OWN loop. But for character arrays, you can just give cin the name of the array and it will use its own INTERNAL loop to receive all characters the user types and store them sequentially in the array. So, internally it is actually looping over the characters so you don't have to. It just assumes when you give it a character array that you WANT it to get a full string (stopping at the next space). cin treats character arrays specially. Code example: int data[5]; char str1[8]; int sum = 0; cin >> data; // won't even compile. // right way to get int array contents: for(int i=0; i<5; i++){ cin >> data[i]; } cin >> str1; Memory diagrams show str1 before input with garbage values ('?') and sum=0, then after user types 'CS102', str1 contains 'C','S','1','0','2','\0' with remaining positions as garbage.
notes_text: cin stops reading at whitespace. This is an important limitation - it cannot read strings with spaces using the >> operator.

images.description: Two memory state diagrams showing str1 before and after cin input. Before: all positions contain '?' (garbage) with sum=0. After user types 'CS102': positions [0]-[4] contain 'C','S','1','0','2', position [5] has '\0', remaining positions still garbage.

title: A Problem with cin and Character Arrays
summary: Demonstrates the buffer overflow danger when cin reads more characters than a character array can hold, and introduces C++ strings as the solution.
main_text: A Problem with cin and Character Arrays. What if the user types in TOO much (more characters than our array has room to store)? cin will not stop! It will keep storing the characters the user types, overwriting whatever data and variables came after the array. Warning: cin does not CHECK that the string typed by the user will fit in the array; instead it simply overwrites memory leading to undefined (bad) behavior! C++ strings fix this issue, allocating more space based on what is typed. Code example: int main() { char str1[4]; int sum = 0; cin >> str1; cout << sum << endl; // won't see 0 because sum was modified when cin received the string that was too long! string s2; cin >> s2; // works regardless of user input length. } Memory diagrams show str1 with 4 slots and sum, then after user types 'CS102', str1 overflows into sum's memory: 'C','S','1','0','2','\0'...
notes_text: This is a critical security and correctness issue known as buffer overflow. C++ strings dynamically resize to avoid this problem.

images.description: Memory diagrams showing buffer overflow: str1 has only 4 bytes at addresses 520-523, with sum at address 524. When user types 'CS102' (5 chars + null), the string overflows past str1 into sum's memory location, corrupting the sum variable.

title: What About Other Operations
summary: Shows that comparing character arrays with == does not work, requiring manual element-by-element loops, and motivates the introduction of the C++ string type.
main_text: What About Other Operations. How would you check whether two strings (character arrays) are equal (i.e. have the same character sequence)? Since we can only do 1 thing at a time, we'd have to use a loop. Does '==' have a special relationship with character arrays? NO!!! Most operations on strings require a loop since we can only do 1 thing at a time. cin and cout are exceptions. Every other operation requires the programmer to write a loop! So, when C++ came along they said, let's fix this. Let's provide code to deal with strings. Enter the C++ string type. Code example: char str1[7] = "CS 102"; char str2[7] = "CS 103"; if(str1 == str2) { ... } // Doesn't work. // Instead you'd need some kind of loop: bool same = true; for(int i=0; /* some condition */; i++) { if(str1[i] != str2[i]) { same = false; } } Memory shows str1 and str2 side by side at addresses 520-526, both containing similar characters but differing at index [5]: '2' vs '3'.
notes_text: The == operator on character arrays compares memory addresses, not string contents. This is a common source of bugs for beginners.

images.description: Memory diagram showing two character arrays str1 and str2 stored in computer memory at addresses 520-526, each containing 'C','S',' ','1','0' but differing at index [5]: str1 has '2' and str2 has '3', both ending with '\0'.

title: C-Strings != C++ strings
summary: Comparison table contrasting C-Strings (character arrays) with C++ strings across constants, variables, includes, I/O, and available operations.
main_text: C-Strings != C++ strings. Comparison table: As constants (same): C-String uses "hi", C++ String uses "hi". As variables (different): C-String uses char str1[3] = "hi"; char str2[4] = "bye";. C++ String uses string str1 = "hi"; string str2 = "bye";. To use: C-String requires No special #include. C++ String requires #include <string>. Works with cout: C-String Yes!, C++ String Yes!. Works with cin: C-String Yes, but potentially dangerous. C++ String Yes!. Other ops: C-String None. C++ String supports Reassignment, Comparison (==, <, >, etc.), Substrings. Why are strings messy? Because they are variable length, where as other variable types are a fixed size! Any int can fit in the memory of another int variable. But for strings what if we want to store a new, longer string in the memory of a shorter string? We don't have room?
notes_text: This is a key reference slide. The fundamental issue is that strings are variable-length data, unlike fixed-size types like int or double.

title: Character Arrays and Strings (2)
summary: Demonstrates that C++ strings can do everything character arrays can do, with code showing both types used side by side for output, modification, and input.
main_text: Character Arrays and Strings (2). C++ strings can do everything that character arrays can do. Code example: int main() { char str2[7] = "CS 102"; string str3 = "CS 102"; cout << str2 << endl; // prints "CS 102". cout << str3 << endl; // prints "CS 102". str2[5] = '3'; str3[5] = '3'; cout << str2 << endl; // prints "CS 103". cout << str3 << endl; // prints "CS 103". cin >> str2; // get a new string from the user (suppose user types "hello"). cin >> str3; cout << str2; cout << str3; return 0; } Program Output: CS 102, CS 102, CS 103, CS 103, hello, hello. Memory diagram shows str2 at addresses 520-526 containing 'C','S',' ','1','0','2','\0'.
notes_text: This slide proves that switching from char arrays to C++ strings requires minimal code changes while gaining significant benefits.

images.description: Memory diagram showing str2 character array at addresses 520-526, indices [0]-[6], containing 'C','S',' ','1','0','2','\0'.

metadata.topic: C++ string compatibility with char arrays

title: C++ Strings
summary: Introduces the C++ string type with its do's and don'ts, including #include <string>, no size declaration needed, array-style indexing, and safe cin input.
main_text: C++ Strings. In C++, the library adds a new object type named string (C++) and provides an easier alternative to working with plain-old character arrays (C-language). Do's and Don'ts: Do #include <string>. Don't need to declare the size (i.e. [7]), just assign. Do still use it like an array by using [index] to get individual characters. Do still use cin/cout with strings. Don't worry about how many characters the user types when inputting to a C++ string. Code example: #include <iostream> #include <string> using namespace std; int main() { char str1[7] = "CS 102"; string str2 = "CS 102"; str1[5] = '3'; // now str1 = "CS 103". str2[5] = '4'; // now str2 = "CS 104". cout << str1 << endl; // prints "CS 103". cout << str2 << endl; // prints "CS 104". cin >> str1; // If the user types more than 6 chars..uh oh! cin >> str2; // str2 will adjust to hold whatever the user types. }
notes_text: The key advantage is that C++ strings handle memory management automatically, eliminating buffer overflow risks present with character arrays.

title: What Do Strings Do
summary: Explains that C++ strings abstract character arrays behind the scenes and demonstrates string concatenation using the + operator.
main_text: What Do Strings Do. strings simply abstract character arrays. Behind the scenes strings are just creating and manipulating character arrays but giving you a simplified set of operators and functions. Can concatenate (append) to a string with the + operator. Code example: #include <iostream> #include <string> using namespace std; int main() { string str2 = "CS 102"; // str2 stores 6 chars. = "CS 102". str2 = "Computer Science"; // now str2 stores 16 characters. // Can append using '+' or '+=' operator. str2 = str2 + " is cool"; // now str2 stores 24 characters. } The diagram shows str2 as an object containing a pointer (value 24 for size) that points to successive plain-old character arrays: first "CS 102", then "Computer Science", then "Computer Science is cool". Each time the string is reassigned or appended, a new character array is allocated.
notes_text: The + operator for strings is an example of operator overloading in C++. The string object manages memory allocation and deallocation automatically.

images.description: Diagram showing how the str2 string object works internally. The str2 box contains a pointer (showing value 24) that points to successive character arrays. Three states shown: 'CS 102' (crossed out), 'Computer Science' (crossed out), and 'Computer Science is cool' (current). Each is labeled as 'Plain-old character array'.

title: String Size
summary: Introduces the .size() member function for C++ strings, which returns the number of real characters excluding the null terminator.
main_text: String Size. Strings track how many characters they are storing. Call the <stringname>.size() function to get the string's size. Returns the actual number of real characters (and does not count overhead like the null character). Code example: #include <iostream> #include <string> using namespace std; int main() { string str2 = "CS 102"; cout << str2.size() << endl; // 6. str2 = "Computer Science"; cout << str2.size() << endl; // 16. str2 = str2 + " is cool"; cout << str2.size() << endl; // 24. }
notes_text: The .size() function is essential for loops that process strings character by character. It returns the count of visible characters, not including the internal null terminator.

title: String Comparison
summary: Explains that comparison operators do not work with C-Strings but do work with C++ strings, performing lexicographic (dictionary-order) comparison.
main_text: String Comparison. Comparison operators do not work with plain old character arrays (C-Strings). C++ strings do perform lexicographic (alphabetical/dictionary-order) comparison when comparison operators (<, >, ==, etc.) are applied. Examples: "a" < "z" ? T/F. "a" > "aa" ? T/F. "ab" < "ba" ? T/F. "aab" < "aac" ? T/F. Code example: #include <iostream> #include <string> using namespace std; int main() { char str1[4] = "abc"; string str2 = "abc"; if( str1 == "abc" ) // doesn't work {...} if( str2 == "abc" ) // works..true {...} if( str1 < "aac" ) // doesn't work {...} if( str2 < "aac" ) // works..false {...} string str3 = "acb"; if( str3 > str2 ) // works..true {...} }
notes_text: Lexicographic comparison compares character by character using ASCII values. This slide presents quiz-style T/F questions without revealing answers, saving those for the solutions section.

title: Substrings
summary: Introduces the .substr() function for extracting portions of C++ strings, with two overloaded versions: one-argument and two-argument forms.
main_text: Substrings. C++ strings allow you to produce a new string from a substring of a current string. Call either of the 2 versions: .substr(start_index) or .substr(start_index, length) function on the string. 1st version generates substring from starting index location all the way to the end of the string. 2nd version generates substring from the starting index and includes the next 'length' characters. Note: when a function has the same name but different options for parameters we say the function is overloaded. Returns a new string. Even if length is 1 (i.e. if length is 1 you might think you just get a char, but you still get a string). Code example: int main() { string str1 = "CS102"; string str2 = str1.substr(2); // str2 = "102". str1 = "Hello World"; str2 = str1.substr(6,2); // str2 = "Wo". str2 = str1.substr(0,1); // str2 = "H". }
notes_text: The substr function is one of the most commonly used string operations. Note that the second parameter is length, not an end index.

title: String Comparison Solutions
summary: Provides the answers to the lexicographic string comparison exercises: reveals that all four comparisons evaluate to TRUE or FALSE.
main_text: String Comparison (Solutions). Comparison operators do not work with plain old character arrays (C-Strings). C++ strings do perform lexicographic (alphabetical/dictionary-order) comparison when comparison operators (<, >, ==, etc.) are applied. Answers: "a" < "z" ? TRUE. "a" > "aa" ? FALSE. "ab" < "ba" ? TRUE. "aab" < "aac" ? TRUE. Code example: #include <iostream> #include <string> using namespace std; int main() { char str1[4] = "abc"; string str2 = "abc"; if( str1 == "abc" ) // doesn't work {...} if( str2 == "abc" ) // works..true {...} if( str1 < "aac" ) // doesn't work {...} if( str2 < "aac" ) // works..false {...} string str3 = "acb"; if( str3 > str2 ) // works..true {...} }
notes_text: Explanations: "a" < "z" is TRUE because 'a' has a lower ASCII value than 'z'. "a" > "aa" is FALSE because "a" is a prefix of "aa" and shorter strings come first. "ab" < "ba" is TRUE because 'a' < 'b' at index 0. "aab" < "aac" is TRUE because at index 2, 'b' < 'c'.
